utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in the courtroom. Good morning. At the outset of today's hearing, the Chamber would like to raise three procedural matters. The first is related to replacement of draft transcripts again. The Chamber wishes to clarify its previous oral order of the 3rd of May concerning the replacement of draft transcripts headed: "Not Official; Not Corrected." Although the draft transcripts specified for replacement in the previous order were the public versions, the Chamber considers that it is in the interests of justice to have all draft transcripts, whether public or confidential, replaced by the official, corrected versions. This means that, in addition to those transcripts specified in our previous order, the Prosecution should liaise with the Registry to also replace the following confidential draft transcripts with the official versions: P1, P8, P20, P48, P59, P68, P96, and P101, and any other draft transcripts that are subsequently identified. Furthermore, the Chamber notes that in the future, draft transcripts tendered into evidence will only be provisionally admitted and marked for identification, pending replacement by the official versions. The second matter is related to tendered materials. The Chamber takes this opportunity to remind the parties that pursuant to the 24th of February, 2010, order on presentation of evidence and as explained in the trial management meeting held on the 5th of March this year, this is an e-court trial. As such, the documents in e-court comprise the official evidentiary record of the proceedings. Therefore, a party tendering a document into evidence should make every effort to ensure that the document is up-loaded and released in e-court as of the date of tendering. This is the date a party moves on the record for admission of a document into evidence, whether done orally in court or filed in a written submission. Furthermore, as of the date of tendering, the parties shall not modify the tendered document without leave of the Chamber. The exceptions to this rule occur in the very limited circumstances when the Chamber has admitted an exhibit pending the attachment of a translation, or ordered the parties to replace draft transcripts with the official versions. In these instances, leave of the Chamber has already been granted for the tendering party to liaise with the Registry to modify the tendered documents. All other modifications of tendered documents must be approved by the Chamber. The third matter is related to today's witness. And before the witness is brought in, the Chamber would like to note one procedural matter concerning this witness. Yesterday, the Chamber orally and partially granted the Prosecution's motion filed on the 26th of April, in which it requested to convert the next witness, Danko Gojkovic, from a 92 bis witness to a 92 ter witness. In this regard, the Chamber notes that in the Prosecution's notification on its witnesses scheduled for this week, filed last Friday, the 11th of June, Gojkovic was listed simply as a 92 ter witness, without indicating that his evidence was still subject to a decision on the motion. Just before the end of the session yesterday, the Prosecution notified that the status of Gojkovic's evidence was still pending. In the Chamber's view, such a last-minute notice is not preferable and could be unfair, even though the accused did not oppose the Prosecution's request in this particular instance. In addition, the Chamber noticed that Witness Gojkovic is not included in the Prosecution's list of witnesses scheduled for this month. Therefore, the Chamber encourages that in the future, a timely notification be made so that the Chamber could issue a decision appropriately and expeditiously. These were some guide-lines, and now the witness should be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down. Mr. McCloskey, for the Prosecution, has some questions for you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you first, Witness, please state your name for the record?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Danko Gojkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you spell the last name so we get it right?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: G-O-J-K-O-V-I-C.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Yesterday, did you get a chance, in our offices, to listen to your testimony in the Popovic case that you gave in April and May of 2007?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. At this point, I would like to offer the previous testimony into evidence, and it is number P496.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY

However, some of those documents were mentioned in Tomasz Blaszczyk's direct testimony in this case when he was talking about the Drina Corps collection, because these documents are also from the Drina Corps collection, and so you will -- I think you should see on your list, in bold on the left side, those numbers that were previously given to some of Mr. Gojkovic's documents because they were discussed, in part, by Mr. Blaszczyk. And when I reviewed each of the documents now, I noticed that the first three or four documents in the packet, he did not actually speak of in his previous interview, but I just wanted to clarify that. I still think all these documents should come in because they were part of this packet that was found separately in the Drina Corps collection. And given that it appears there is a challenge on some important documents, I think it's important that the Court has the entire packet so that they can look at it as a whole. And so that said, I would offer that packet of documents in their entirety as they came in in the Popovic case, and all their numbers you should have now that were assigned by the Registry. And I'm at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you are referring to the numbers P468 through P495.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's correct. And we already see that there is -- the Blaszczyk documents were P122, 128, 123, 124, 129 and 125.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That's correct, and these documents will be received. And I hope they all have a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, they do, although I noticed a few glitches here and there in some of the translations; nothing major. Some of them, I will be able to fix, and we'll be notifying the Court of anything serious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was told by the Registry they all have an attached translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, they do. And I'm told that the Popovic transcript is the proper revised, full transcript, so we should be in good shape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I will read a brief summary of your evidence. Mr. Danko Gojkovic was born in June 1967 in Rogatica, Bosnia and Herzegovina. He performed his mandatory military service in 1985 in the JNA in the Communications Section. He was mobilised in April 1992 and worked as a signalsman in the Command of the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade, known informally as the Rogatica Brigade. In July 1995, Gojkovic was working as a teleprinter operator in the Communications Platoon of the Rogatica Brigade. At the time, he worked with other teleprinter operators, including an older man he knew by the name of Ziza. Gojkovic described his duties and the system of receiving and transmitting encrypted communications between his unit and other VRS units. As a teleprinter operator, Gojkovic would be brought various documents or telegrams, either typed or handwritten or received orally over the telephone, and he would type them into the teleprinter and then transmit them in an encrypted form to the appropriate location. After he typed a message into the teleprinter, he would sign and date either the original message or the typewritten version that came out of the teleprinter and send it back to the command. He also received documents sent to the Rogatica Brigade over the teleprinter. When Gojkovic received a document addressed to the Rogatica Brigade Command on the teleprinter, he would write on the top of the document the time and date when it was received and then sign it. He or another person would then deliver it to the Rogatica Brigade Command. Gojkovic also described the process of coding and decoding transmissions and how couriers and other forms of communications were employed to transmit information and orders up and down the chain of command. In his interview with the OTP on 16 May 2006, Gojkovic was shown a package of documents related to the Rogatica Brigade Command that was found in the Drina Corps collection. Gojkovic commented upon whether or not he recognised his initials or signatures on these documents. Gojkovic did not know or recall anything regarding the substance of these documents, but did identify his initials and those of some others. These documents included reports sent to General Tolimir at the Rogatica Command in July 1995 and included reports authored by General Tolimir and sent out from the Rogatica Command in July 1995. Among the documents he was shown was document ERN 0525-8580, dated 13 July 1995, under the name of Lieutenant-Colonel Milomir Savcic and noted to have been from the IKM of the 65th Protection Regiment at Borike, sent to the commander of the VRS Main Staff. The document was titled "Procedure for the treatment of prisoners of war." Gojkovic confirmed that he typed the document into the teleprinter and sent it. He identified his handwriting at the bottom of the page of the document, indicating the dispatch time of 1510 hours and the date of 13 July 1995 and his signature. Gojkovic could not recall whether he was given this document by a courier or over the telephone. Gojkovic stated that there was no teleprinter connection between his office at the Rogatica Command and the forward command post at Borike. However, there was a telephone communication between his office and Borike. Gojkovic also stated that the Borike IKM did not have a teleprinter, meaning that the Borike IKM would not have sent any documents via teleprinter directly from the Borike IKM. And that concludes my summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Gojkovic, did you, in listening to that, find any mistakes I made?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: You did not make any mistakes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't get a translation because I didn't have it on the right channel. Could you -- I'll just read that. Pardon me. Okay. Now, just to clarify, as a teleprinter operator, can you just describe to us what a teleprinter machine is, just in the most basic terms? We're familiar with fax machines, most of us remember old typewriters, but can you describe to us, just in the simplest terms, so we can visualise what this machine is that you're operating?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: A teleprinter is like an electronic typewriter. It sends and receives telegrams, and that the keyboard is the same like on a computer, except it's -- I don't know how to else to explain it. Only if we --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, that's fine. And I'll go over four documents with you, and we can help explain it that way as well. And so if we could go to the first document, and this would be P490. And let me ask you, do you remember the substance or information in any of these documents where you identified your signature and that of others?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. In that event, Your Honours, while the substance may be of interest, I will be concentrating with this witness on the B/C/S version, where he'll be identifying various things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so if you could look at what's on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could we bring the B/C/S version a bit down so we can get -- I'm sorry, the other direction. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us what this document is? We see that it's a -- you know, it's a printed document in all caps, mostly, with some handwriting on it. What is this, just -- does this have anything to do with the teleprinter?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was this document received or sent by you?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I sent it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: In the top right corner, it's written "2315 of 15 July 1995," and my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what does that mean, that time, date, and your signature, in relation to this document?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: It's the time when the telegram was received at the corps, and they confirmed receipt.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, and you say "the corps." How do you know it was received at the corps and not -- we also see it's addressed to the GS VRS, the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: On the other side, there is also a teleprinter operator, and he typed back that he received the telegram. That's the only connection I have with the corps. I worked everything -- I worked -- I did all of my work for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I understand that. Is there any way that you can tell from your notes that you actually received word back from the corps, as opposed to one of the other addressees on the document?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No, there isn't anything. I got it on a piece of paper, typed on the teleprinter, and I wrote down the time on the telegram.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And can you -- did you originally get this document and type it into the teleprinter to send it off to the addressees?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this particular document that we're looking at, since it has your signature on it, where did it actually come from? After you typed the document -- a document into the teleprinter, where does this document come from? Is this the original document you were given or is this a document that came out of the teleprinter?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: This was typed into the teleprinter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, if we could go to the bottom of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, we can see, from the bottom of the document, that it was from Rajko Kusic and M. Savcic, but there is no -- there is no signature. So is it possible, like it is with a fax machine, to send a signature over a teleprinter?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: You cannot send a signature like that. Everything that's written on the piece of paper I typed into the teleprinter, but you cannot actually transmit a signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you get an important document like this document, would it normally have a signature on it before you actually typed the document into the teleprinter to send it?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No, it didn't need to have a signature. I really cannot remember whether it was supposed to have one or not, but for the most part there was no signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to another document, P123. And while we are waiting for that to come up, when you were shown these documents in the interview, were you shown the actual originals with actual inked signatures on your part; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We have those originals here, if you would like to -- if you think you need to consult them at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, we have those, if you think that is necessary at any point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And now, looking at this document, we see in the English up on the right, and we see in the Serbian up in the right, it looks like handwritten Cyrillic, and in the English it says "Ziza." Who or what is Ziza; can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: He was also a teleprinter operator when I worked there. Actually, he was the one who trained me. He was an older man, but I cannot really tell you until when he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recall telling us in the interview that you thought that he had left before you or that you had replaced him during this time-period?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I do, but I made a mistake. He was there, and he left -- perhaps if we had more of these telegrams, then we could see exactly when he left, but I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In my office yesterday, were you shown the packet of telegrams, where you had a chance to look at the telegrams from July and see Ziza's name on some of them?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I mentioned a name of a person yesterday to you. I asked you if the name Desimir Zizovic sounded at all familiar. And can you tell us whether it does?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is that -- does that have any relation to the Ziza you've been talking about?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And now looking at the -- let's look at the bottom of this document. We see "Ziza" written in -- at the right-hand corner on the top, and at the bottom of the B/C/S -- I think we need to go to the next page of the English -- sorry, and the third page of the English to get the end of the document. We see there, down at the bottom, the initials "DZ." It's actually typed in. Can you tell us who that is?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't really say, but I think these are Ziza's initials, "DZ."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Would it be normal for the teleprinter operator to put their initials at the bottom of the teleprinted document like this?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Actually, if I remember correctly, I think it was not allowed. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we see, in the Serbian version, it says "Predato," it looks like, and then an hour. Can you just read that to us, what you see, "Predato," and what you think that says?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: "Received" or "Handed in" at 950 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't know how well you remember the handwriting. Is it possible that "00,50," that's just what the translator saw, but you're the best person to be able to give us guidance. Can you -- do you have an opinion on which way that would be?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps it is "0050." I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the next --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you leave this page, I would just like to indicate, for the record, in the B/C/S version it's "D.ZZ." Perhaps you could clarify why this is a double Z in comparison to the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If you could focus on again those letters that we see, "D.ZZ." Do you have -- can you help explain to us why there would be two Zs if this was what you thought it was, Ziza's initials?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know why there is a double Z. I am not sure. Perhaps that's how he signed himself. I don't know why there are two letters Z.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you think of any other reason, not related to Ziza, why there would be letters like this, some other related reasons in identifying the document, or the machine, or just some reason not related to teleprinter operator?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, there was no letter "Zh" on the teleprinter, so I don't know why he put a double Z.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the letter "Zh" has a diacritic indicating the sound "Zh," is that correct, and that's not on the teleprinter?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: That is true, it did not have that letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Mindua has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A small question. Witness, is there a reason to think that this word "Predato 00,50" -- or could it be "0950"? Is there a reason that it should be one or the other? Because in English, what is translated is "0050," without a comma and without a "9."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I didn't understand the question. Could you please repeat it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll start again. On the bottom of the B/C/S page, it says, handwritten "Predato," and the translation we have in the English text is "Handwritten/0050 hrs," "hours." I'm wondering the following: Could it be "00,50," as Mr. McCloskey seems to think or said, or "0950," 9 hours 50 minutes instead of 0 hours and 50 minutes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't really know if it's "0050" or "0950." I really cannot tell, either, whether it's a "0," or a "9."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. President, I think it would be helpful if the Trial Chamber and the witness were able to see this and make your own judgement. It's one of those judgement calls, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps first for Mr. Tolimir and Mr. Gajic, and then to the witness. Please show it to the witness now. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Gojkovic, can you give us your best opinion on what you think that says?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I'm able to answer this question. It could be "0050" or "0950." I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that. And I would note, for the record, that we can see that the English translation, while it got the time, it did not get "Predato," but I think the witness has clarified what that means, and I think it would be a good idea if we sent that to be revised so that they do get that in the record, so we don't have to go back to the transcript to figure it out, or a dictionary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And then the document could be given back to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now can we go to P49 [sic] and take a look at that for a moment. P491.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to avoid an error in the transcript, the following document actually says when it was transmitted, so my assistant can show you the document and give you the ERN number so you can establish, on the basis of that time, the time of this document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is that something to be dealt with in cross-examination or would it be helpful, for your line of questions, that Mr. Gajic is given the ERN number?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I -- there's many ways to figure out times and orders. You can look at the numbers. Other documents are numbered afterwards, so there are very many interesting and investigative ways of sorting this out. The General is absolutely correct. I have no problem with them showing that to us, but it may be better on cross. I'm not sure what he means, but if it's something you want to sort out right now, that's fine as well; either way. These are just meant to be a few examples of the kind of documents he's marking, but they will be, of course, the subject of analysis of other witnesses, expert witnesses and other folks. But anything we can resolve, the sooner the better, in my view, but I think he's got a better handle on that right now than I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was only wondering if it would disturb your line of questions. Mr. Gajic, please do what Mr. Tolimir was suggesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, Your Honour. I would just like to say that we can establish whether it says "0050" here or "0950" here. We can look at Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel kindly be asked to repeat the exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And we will see the manner in which Ziza wrote the dates in the document, the date and the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Gajic, you are the champion in the speed of speaking. The interpreters didn't catch your -- the number you have given. Please repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we could look at Exhibit P489, since in this document, at the lower right-hand corner, the time is indicated, and it is very probable that this marking was entered by Ziza again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We should have it on the screen, and we can then put a question to the witness on that. Thank you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't see how that's very helpful. It is another Ziza document, and we agree with that. It's part of the material we're offering into evidence. I can ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Witness, do you see Ziza having done something on this document?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And would he have -- do you know who would have written "Predato" and the time in the bottom right-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that it is Ziza, because also there is his signature in the upper right-hand corner. So it's probably him. I don't know who else it could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in looking at the way he wrote his numbers for the time, does that help you sort out what the time in the previous document might have been?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No. You can see clearly the numbers, and there it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Perhaps let me ask you one thing about this document. It may or may not be helpful, but looking in the left-hand corner, where you see the abbreviation for "Strictly Confidential," "number 04-520-58/95," what is that?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: The number of the telegram, most probably, and that before it came to the teleprinter, it was probably logged into some kind of record or log-book. I really cannot remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Would such a number be sequential, meaning would it change each time another document came in, in the order that the documents either came in or were sent out?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do think it changed with each following dispatch.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. If we could go to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could we please go to the bottom again of both versions. And I think in English, the next page. In B/C/S, we see the date, 17th July, and then the time, "0120," without a comma in between. Witness, what was usual, if you write a time, to put a comma between the hour and the minutes or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it just depends on the way people would usually enter such information. I would put a colon, somebody would put a comma, somebody would put a dash. It depends. I really cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Staying on this issue, could we go to 492. And if I could hand the Court the original, and, of course, for the General and for the witness. And if we could put that up on the screen as well, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It should be shown to the accused and Mr. Gajic, and then to the witness, and then back to Mr. McCloskey. We saw the original document and saw there was a comma included. That's all what we can see from that document. And if you can scroll down or go to the last page. Thank you. And the same in English, please, last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Gojkovic, if we could just get your opinion on what time you believe this is, based on your experience, having worked there?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: In this telegram, "0100." "0100," 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you see which teleprinter operator did that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The document disappeared from the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the right upper corner, again it says "Ziza."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we go to the first page of the English to see if -- make sure the translation caught that. Yes, I see it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so in your view, looking at that number down at the bottom, is that a comma, in your view?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to 492, if we could, please. I'm sorry, let's go to 491, which is part of my regularly scheduled, second-to-last document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe has a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: I have a question for Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Is Ziza available to you as a witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, he is, Your Honour, and we have interviewed him and he should be available. He's not on our witness list, but as we see what is contested and what issues there are, we were thinking that that might be a good idea, but we're not absolutely sure yet because we're not sure how many of the documents there will be a contest to. But, yes, he is available, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Looking at this document, do you see your handwriting on it anywhere?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: In the right top corner, my signature and my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so were you the person that wrote "Sent at 1820 hours on 13 July," and then signed your name?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And let's go to the bottom of the document, page 3 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see -- can you look at the letters "G.D." down at the bottom left corner, and tell us what you think that is.

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: My initials.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So that would be "Gojkovic, Danko," I take it.

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is starting with the last name first a customary way of putting one's initials sometimes in the former Yugoslavia, like this?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I typed "G.D." It could have been also "D.G."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what kind of a machine was this document created from?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: You mean the document I'm looking at?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: The teleprinter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how can you tell that?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was typed on a teleprinter. It's typed as a telegram. I believe it's a teleprinter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we noticed there is no handwritten signature at the bottom, and can you explain why that is?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: It was at the top of the telegram. You could write it at the top or at the bottom. It didn't matter. What was important was that there was a signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we have the witness look at this -- the original of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Does this sort of long, narrow shape and the paper help you sort out what kind of machine this came from?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: It doesn't help me. I don't know what type it is. There were two types of teleprinters. I really can't say which one it is. I'm afraid to make a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't need to know which actual type of teleprinter, but can you conclude it is a teleprinter, as opposed to a typewriter, or a fax, or something else?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: This is certainly a teleprinter paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you ever use a fax machine in your work in 1995?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Not that I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Can you -- is this a document that you did?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I only typed it and transmitted it. I didn't create the document. Somebody brought it to me. I retyped it and sent it where it needed to be sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So this is a machine -- this document came out of the teleprinter machine at the Rogatica Brigade after you typed it in; correct?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know, what would you have done with the original document that you used to create this? For example, if General Tolimir brought you something either handwritten or typewritten, what would you have done with that original that was brought to you by him or his subordinates or couriers?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I would return it to the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Hold on to that document for one second. Let's go to the last document, and I want to give you the original of that, and that is P125. This was the document that was the subject of the 92 ter and my summary, so I -- but it is a rather important document. And if we could show the original to the witness. And I don't know if the General or Mr. Gajic wants to see it first. They're, of course, welcome to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please give it first to Mr. Tolimir and Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And if you could just study that for a minute. Again, I'm not interested in the substance of this document, but could you just hold both documents up so that we can get a good look at them, one in one hand and one in the other? I just want to get an idea of the shape so we can see the different shape of the two documents. Okay.

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. The document that we're now talking about is clearly much more rectangular than the previous document. Can you tell us the -- okay, thank you very much for that. The document that you're looking at right now, 125, what kind of -- we see that that is a -- we see typeface on this. What kind of machine did this document, in your view?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: In my opinion, a typewriter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you have anything to do with this document?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What I mean by that is: Do you recognise any writing you did on this document?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I wrote that I transmitted it at 1510 hours on the 13th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is that an original inked signature of yours in the bottom left-hand corner underneath that information you just gave us?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you sometimes use a typewriter in your job in 1995?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you have access to a typewriter around the command somewhere?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: There was certainly a typewriter at the command. But where I worked, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you recall whether or not you received this information over the phone and had it typed in or whether someone delivered you this particular document and you typed it into the teleprinter? Do you know which way it was?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember. I think they brought it to me to retype. I don't think it's likely that somebody dictated it over the phone for someone else to type it and then bring it to me to retype.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If someone was in -- at the Borike Forward Command Post and wanted a message sent by you, could they dictate it over the telephone for you to write it down and send it?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they could, but as far as I remember, that didn't happen because there was a telephone connection with Borike.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was there any teleprinter connection or fax connection with Borike, where they could actually send you a document already done?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, there was no teleprinter at Borike, and even less likely a fax machine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We can see, from this document which has your original inked signature on it, that it does not have any signature on the -- from the author by the document, Commander Lieutenant-Colonel Milomir Savcic. Can you make -- can you comment on that, why there is no signature?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I don't have an explanation, and there's no signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There's also no strictly confidential number, and it's, as we can see, not in the typical form of a -- that we've seen from the other teleprinter documents. Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't explain it. If only we had this same document typed on a teleprinter with a number on it, or perhaps I made a telephone call to find out the number. If we had the teleprinter version of this document, we would see perhaps a number, or perhaps it was sent simply like this, without a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But the fact that you have signed and written "Delivered" on this, does that indicate that you actually typed this into a teleprinter and sent it?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, you know that now the accused has the possibility to put questions to you. Mr. Tolimir, do you have cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Peace unto this house, peace unto everyone. I hope that this day of trial and the entire trial and the entire process be completed as God wills it, not as I will it. I do have questions for this witness, and I will put them now, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, since we speak the same language, when I say, Thank you, at the end of the question, then please wait a couple of seconds, and you can follow the typing on the screen in front of you. Wait until the typing finishes and then start answering, to avoid overlapping. Thank you. My first question is: In July 1995, you worked at the command of the Rogatica Brigade. How far was that command from the forward command post at Borike? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Eighteen kilometres, if you go on the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Make just a slightly longer pause before your answer. Mr. Gojkovic, you talked to the Prosecutor on 16 May 2005, at the field office of the ICTY in Sarajevo, and also now in preparation for this testimony, and other times you testified before this Tribunal, and you constantly discussed the same series of documents. Did you call this set of documents "Atlantis" or did the Prosecutor give it that name?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I was also told that the batch is called "Atlantis," but I personally don't know what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you say for the transcript that you did not write, yourself, this name "Atlantis" that is indicated here together with the ERN number?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not write that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us where those telegrams that you and Ziza transmitted were kept and who had access to them in your teleprinter room?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: They were in our keeping. And when we were done with them, we returned them to the command. We didn't keep them longer than the time we needed to type them and transmit them. They would be immediately returned to the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And where did you keep teleprinter tapes that were an impression of the telegrams that you transmitted?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: We would have one or two tapes. The others were kept somewhere in the depot or the command. I can't remember exactly where. But we always had one in use and one in reserve, just in order not to run out during one shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Where were the copies of teleprinter tapes for already-sent, outgoing telegrams kept, and for how long were they kept, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they were kept for 24 or 48 hours. I can't remember. Then they were destroyed. I don't know exactly how long. We kept them for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In your training to become a teleprinter operator, were you taught that these tapes had to be kept as proof that a telegram was sent?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said. They were kept for a day or two just in case a problem occurred, and then they were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know they should not have been destroyed until the competent person, official, who gave you the code allowed it? They should not have been destroyed?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know that a text typed on a teleprinter, on a perforated tape and on this narrow paper, must not be allowed to fall into the hands of the enemy, who could use it to discover your codes?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know that it is also prohibited to misappropriate both the perforated tape and the teleprinter copy that you can produce to the command as proof of sending?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you repeat that question? I didn't really understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know that teleprinter material, in the form of a perforated tape, and the copy that is obtained after typing on a keyboard, the keyboard of the teleprinter, must not be destroyed or given to other persons so they -- or, rather, lest they discover your codes based on the perforated tape?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's true, we were not supposed to give it to anyone. It was not allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is it the case that every teleprinter machine releases both a perforated tape and a paper with the characteristic typing?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: The teleprinter, yes. The teleprinter runs both the perforated tape and the paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did all your teleprinters write telegrams mostly in those large block letters or small letters?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how to answer that. There were two types of teleprinters. This is, for instance, one type. I can't remember exactly the typing of the other one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All these telegrams shown you by the Prosecutor that you saw yesterday and earlier today, were they written -- typed in big block letters?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: The one currently on the screen is. The other one, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The other one was not typed on a teleprinter, only a typewriter?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Only typewriter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In big or small letters?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: There are both lower case and upper case letters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Which means that it was typed on a typewriter, not a teleprinter?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you just say to the Prosecutor that you did not have and did not need a typewriter?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: In my work-place, I had no use for a typewriter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Didn't you just say that there was no need for you to type any material brought to you first on a typewriter, then on a teleprinter?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: There was no need for that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank the interpreters for this caution that we are speaking too fast -- that I am speaking too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I will quote. The Prosecutor asked you if you received these telegrams by phone. You said: "No, I don't remember. I think it was brought to me, who would type it on a typewriter and then a teleprinter." Is that what you said a minute ago?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Then I will conclude before this Court that you did not type the contents of this telegram on a typewriter in your workroom. Somebody must have brought it to you.

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I certainly didn't type it on a typewriter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm asking you these questions purposefully while your memory of the direct examination is still fresh. Let me ask you another thing. Is it normal and customary for these telegrams, typed on a machine, to be kept in your documentation, while the perforated tape of the teleprinter is destroyed?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: They didn't need to be kept. As soon as we receive confirmation of receipt from the corps, there was no need to keep it any longer. We kept the tape for 24 or 48 hours - I can't remember which - but we returned the originals immediately to the command as soon as it was typed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: What was to you proof that you sent something from a teleprinter? Was proof this typewritten paper or the tape, perforated in the teleprinter in a specific way, in that specific code? I will repeat my question. For you, as an encryption operator, what was more valid as proof, that you have the perforated tape from that telegram or the copy that the teleprinter machine produced, rather than a typewriter or a manuscript?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: This is for me a confirmation from the other side, from my fellow teleprinter operator on the other side, who confirmed that it was well received.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: If some investigating authorities wanted confirmation that you really sent a particular telegram, would you show them a telegram typewritten on a typewriter or would you show them a teleprinter report and the perforated tape as proof that you sent it?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't produce anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: If they came to you and asked you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey would like the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't want to interrupt the question, but could the record reflect that when he made the answer and said this is -- I don't see exactly where he said it, but this is proof that the other side got it. Could the record reflect that he was holding up -- that's 32, line 7, thank you. Could the record --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Line 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah. Mine says "7," but it says: "This is for me a confirmation from the other side, from my fellow teleprinter operator on the other side, who confirmed that it was well received." Could the record reflect that he picked up the P125, the more rectangular 13 July document, when he made that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Witness, could you confirm what the Prosecutor said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we are over the regular time for the break, so that we should have the first break now. We adjourn and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir. Please carry on with your examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We'll continue where we left off.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, sir, the Prosecutor said this document that you indicated, he noted that for the transcript, did you show the document typed on the teleprinter or typed on the typewriter?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: On the typewriter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And is that document confirmation that the document was sent or the one that was sent out on the teleprinter?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: The one that was sent out on the teleprinter, that is confirmation that it arrived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And is the document of confirmation also the one that was written by the typewriter or something else?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Confirmation for me is the time written on the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I asked you earlier, when investigators come and asked you to prove if you sent the contents of the telegram or not, what would you show them as evidence that you did send the telegram that was given to you? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I would show them the time indicated on the telegram. I would go to the command and find that telegram.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, but you can put in the time after the event. But what would you prove -- what would you show as proof that the telegram was actually sent?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: If I had the tape, if I didn't destroy it, I would take the tape and show that as proof that the telegram was sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: What has more weight, the teleprinter report, the print-out from the teleprinter, or the print-out from the typewriter given to you by the commander?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right, thank you. I will give you an example now. You know that on the 4th of July, 1992, 45 members of the JNA were killed in Zepa, and 31 were wounded, when they tried to provide food to Zlovrh. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Because of the fact that they were killed, Avdo Palic and other persons were charged for killing them. They were from Zepa. They were only trying to provide food to a military facility there, and the teleprinter operator who was dispatching telegrams had to prove that he did send a telegram at Zlovrh that food would arrive, so that these people would not be captured. Thank you. Are you aware of that, these events? Are you aware of these events, because this is close to you?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware that these soldiers were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Are you aware that an investigation was conducted into the way that these people were killed?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Are you aware that the teleprinter was actually the tool that the encryption operator used to prove that there was a telegram sent that food would arrive? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I am not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you aware that only on the basis of this teleprinter print-out, this person was able to prove that the telegram was sent out, because the Muslims had captured Zlovrh, and it was not possible to prove it on the basis of incoming telegrams, but on the basis of outgoing telegrams, and that he couldn't prove that with the document that he was supposed to send out, but he only did that on the basis of the teleprinter copy?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: If you were in a similar situation, what would you provide as proof that you had sent the telegram? Would it be the typewritten copy or the teleprinter print-out? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: If I had the perforated tape, I would provide the teleprinter print-out to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: But if you didn't have the perforated tape, but only the text typewritten on the electronic typewriter or the teleprinter, what would you give me as proof that you did send the telegram? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I really cannot answer. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: If you did send the telegram, would it suffice that you just had something on the typewriter? You could have done that even after the attack on Zlovrh and you could have put it to me as proof.

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know why this would be something that I would be in my -- would have in my safekeeping. We wouldn't keep those. We would return them immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The investigator would consider it more important to have a print-out from the teleprinter, because each -- does each machine have its own characteristics?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And in an investigation or an examination, would you be able to prove whether a paper was printed on a specific typewriter or a teleprinter because of the machine characteristics?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think that somebody could probably be able to establish that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, if you think that's possible, wouldn't it be better to show me the teleprinter print-out, that you had sent the telegram out, or would it be better for you to show me the typewritten text?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the teleprinter print-out would be better.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We're not going to talk about this anymore. Don't be afraid that the Prosecutor and I are putting so many questions to you. I accept every document that you wrote, even the ones that the Prosecutor was trying to prove whether they were drafted on the 9th or not. So just answer calmly and truthfully to my following questions. I'm only putting questions in order to prove the authenticity of the documents, not whether you sent certain documents or not, just like in the example in Zlovrh. You have nothing to be afraid of. All you have to do is answer truthfully. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you should slow down. It's very fast again, and you are overlapping again. Please help the interpreters. Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I apologise to the interpreters for not having that in mind. Can we now please look at Exhibit P468. This is an interview with this witness by Tomasz Blaszczyk, Tribunal investigator, and as well as Julian Nicholls. This is the transcript of the conversation with Danko Gojkovic on the 16th of May, 2005, at the offices of ICTY in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was that when the interview was conducted, at that time?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you please tell me now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we clarify something? I see in the B/C/S version the year 2005, and in the English version the year is 2006. Witness, could you clarify, was it in the year 2005 or 2006?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it was 2005, if I can remember correctly. But I can see that the other document says "2006."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I just wanted to clarify it for the record. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Danko, can you please tell me if you signed any statement when you were interviewed by the investigators from the OTP in Sarajevo on the 16th of May, 2005?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, I didn't sign anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you sign any statement in any contact with the ICTY investigators?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't sign any statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, that's better for you, isn't it? You didn't sign, and they didn't ask you to, so now you can be held responsible for only the things that you said. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at page 5 of this document in the Serbian and page 6 in the English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you see what it says in the second sentence here? You say -- well, the investigator tells you, in line 1: "We will look at this document later. We're looking at 0425-8558." And then you say: "I don't know what that is." So are you clear now about what is said by the investigator and what you said?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, this will be like throughout the whole text, you are marked as "DG"?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And then the OTP investigator says: "We will tell you what that number is. We know that these documents are authentic because we received them directly from Republika Srpska." Do you remember that he told you that?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And then a few lines later, in relation to this same document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One moment. Mr. McCloskey, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It may be a transcription, but the English has that "we received them directly from the VRS," and, of course, there's a very big difference between Republika Srpska and the VRS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Carry on, please, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Danko, please, can you look at line 19?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Where it says -- the Prosecutor says: "Let's go through this document, 0425-8558. I'm looking at the translation." And then he tells you: "You tell me if I'm reading something wrong. 'Sent at 1745 hours, 14th of July, 1995.' And then underneath that, there is your signature." And then after that, you say: "If nobody forged it, then it is." Thank you. Can we now please show -- did you say this? Did I read this correctly?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I didn't turn off -- turn on the microphone. Can we show in e-court 480. Thank you, now we see the document, 480.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In 2005, were you shown this document that Investigator Nicholls says bears your signature?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: On this document, we see only your initials, not your signature; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you can see my initials at the bottom, and in the right top corner there is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: He told you, in the transcript, there is your signature below. We see only your initials, not the signature?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: At the bottom, yes, there are only initials.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does this document bear your signature at the bottom of the document or at the top of the document?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: At the top.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, could you please clarify one thing? The words: "And underneath is your signature; right?", this question of the investigator in the OTP statement, it is referring to the answer -- it is referring to the question before. It says: "Okay. So on the top, and I'm looking at a translation, so you tell me if I read anything wrong. It says: 'Sent 1745 hours, 14th of July, 1995.'" And then the answer of the witness is: "Yes." And then: "And underneath is your signature" -- [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will someone tell me which line it is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is in the English version, lines 12 to 16.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We will look at it. Can we please show page 520 of the first document we were looking at. It's P486, P486. Fifth page, lines 19 through 24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think there's a wrong number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P468, P468, page 5. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We see, in line 19, Nicholls says to you, that's the investigator who talked to you, I quote: "Let us go through this document, 0425-8558. With regard to what is written in this order, explain to us what is the difference between what is written in hand and this document. Before we began, I showed you briefly -- before the interview, I showed you briefly these documents that we will be discussing, and you remembered this. At the top, and I'm looking at the translation, you read me -- you tell me if I'm reading something wrong: 'Sent at 1745 hours, 14th of July, 1995.'" "And underneath is your signature?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, let me just note that this last sentence quoted by Mr. Tolimir, regarding the signature, does not feature in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, you should look first to the answer of the witness, "Yes," and then it continues: "And underneath is your signature; right?" Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, I agree, but in that respect the original and the translation do not correspond entirely, because in the Serbian, line 24, it says: "Sent at 1745 hours on 14 July 1995. "And underneath is your signature." That is in the Serbian version, lines 24 and 25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There is, in fact, the answer "Yes" missing. Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, what do you want to get from the witness? Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Instead of the answer, "Yes," the question asked by the investigator is answered by the witness as follows: "Unless someone falsified it, it is." And the investigator says: "You recognise your signature?" And Mr. Danko says: "I recognise it."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I only wanted to ask you: This answer that you gave, does it relate to some other document which did bear your signature rather than this typewritten document or typed document which does not bear your signature?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We should have it on the screen again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think as you pointed out to him, clearly the signature we're talking about was underneath the date, and so this accusation that Mr. Nicholls is falsely questioning the witness is unfounded and should be withdrawn and made clear to the witness, because the way this is going, he's suggesting to the witness Mr. Nicholls is inappropriately putting words in his mouth. That's absolutely not the case, and he should not go further in those suggestions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think the witness should be shown again this document, and he may comment on the signature we have already seen on the top of this document. I think it was P480, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I kindly ask you that you and the witness and the Prosecutor look at line 19, where the number of the document is indicated, "0425-8558." And he speaks of a signature on some other document, where the typewritten document is P125 and bears the ERN number is 0425-8580. It bears the signature, and that's what the discussion is about. And Danko says after that: "Unless someone falsified it, it is." I'm just pointing out the contents of this interview, and I'm asking the witness about something that's unclear to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We should first have that on the screen, otherwise, it's not very satisfactory to continue in that way.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here, the document is on the screen, and I showed it first to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, and now again ask the witness about the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is there your signature on this document or are there only initials at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: At the bottom, only initials.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you only sign under the indication when the document was sent? You are not signing for the substance of the document?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct, only for when it was sent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm of the opinion that this problem is now solved. Please move on to your next topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not hear the interpretation of what you said because the interpreters were changing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I said, I'm of the opinion that this problem is now solved, and then I said to you, Please move on to your next topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, when this document was shown to you, the one you see on the left side of the screen, did it bear your signature at the bottom of the document or at the top of the document, which only refers to the time of transmission?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: My signature is at the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And what is at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Initials.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Would I be right in saying that one document was shown to you, where there is no signature of yours at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: At the bottom, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please, during the interview in Sarajevo, did investigators tell you and explain how they came into possession of these documents and what the chain of custody was until they reached this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: They got it from someone from Republika Srpska, and that's why I asked if this was perhaps forged, because I'm not aware that we gave them these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please wait.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And do you know that these documents, before being shown to you, were in Serbia, in Mali Zvornik, later in Gornji Milanovac, later in Republika Srpska, and then in Zagreb, and that was the path they travelled?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know that this Prosecutor, who questioned you a moment ago, said himself that one Defence team also had access to these documents while they were in Zvornik and they were not in the control of Republika Srpska authorities?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was that perhaps an opportunity to falsify or replace documents, because they were not under the control of Republika Srpska authorities or your brigade?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: But if you had known then that these documents had been outside of the control of your brigade before they were given to the Prosecutor, would your attitude have been different to the signature on the document?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't have a different attitude. I would have again said it was my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: But can your signature be scanned and copied onto a blank piece of paper; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the technique of scanning a signature from one document to another?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document, the telegram, P125, could it be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This document we see, the typewritten one on the left side, would it have normally had a teleprinter impression if you had transmitted it by teleprinter?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: If they had asked me to put it through the teleprinter, I would have done so. Perhaps they didn't ask for it, I just sent it and returned it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did anyone ever ask you for the teleprinter version of the other telegrams you sent?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Why do all the documents have their teleprinter versions, only this one hasn't?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Why did you keep in archives the teleprinter version of all the documents, all the telegrams, but not this one?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether I had it in my possession, whether I kept it. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Would it be logical, if you sent this telegram also by teleprinter, that it would have a teleprinter impression, like all the telegrams -- all the other telegrams introduced by the Prosecution here?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: It's possibly there somewhere in the Drina Corps. They must have the teleprinter copies. I don't know. How do I know that? It just came to me. I retyped it and sent it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please focus on my question. I'm not accusing you of anything. You said you transmitted it, and I'm asking you: If you really transmitted it, is it logical that every telegram you transmitted has a teleprinter impression, like all the other telegrams the Prosecution is introducing, but not this one?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I know you don't know what to answer, but answer the Trial Chamber. How come that only this telegram does not have a teleprinter copy, just a typewriter copy?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I told you a moment ago they probably didn't want us to give them a teleprinter copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did I ask you for copies for other telegrams?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Not from me. Why would you ask it from me?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Why do they have all the copies of telegrams that I sent, all the other ones?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot answer that either. I don't know. Maybe you asked for the other copies to be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I never asked anything from you, nor have I ever seen you before. Have you seen me before?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Never. I'm 99 per cent sure. I'm leaving the 1 per cent just because I'm not inclined to make it 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you ever speak to me on the phone?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It's logical that you -- that copies were kept for all the other telegrams. It's not your fault, but it should have been done by the archivers of telegrams?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: We returned everything the same second to the command. We kept the teleprinter tape for a day or two or three, and then it would be destroyed.
