utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All these telegrams that we are seeing here that are being introduced through you, that the Prosecutor showed you in direct examination, which are accompanied by teleprinter copies, were they also sent by you to the Documentation Department of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, most of them we sent to the Drina Corps because we liaised with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: They were also your superior command?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were they duty-bound to keep all teleprinter copies for telegrams you sent, but they didn't seem to have kept this one from Savcic?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose they should have kept them. You should ask one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is there a possibility that someone misappropriated the teleprinter copy of this and put in a typewriter copy, or perhaps there is no teleprinter copy for the Savcic telegram at all?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We also see in the transcript of this interview that the Prosecution interrupted you when you said: "I don't know what it is," and they said: "We know these documents are authentic."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could my legal adviser indicate the reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We'll look at it now, and you will see it in the record of your interview. At one point, you say: "I don't know what this is." And they answer: "We know," and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's P468 that we looked at before. Can it be shown again, page 5?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In the English, it's page 6, line 16, where they say: "Well, we know that these documents are authentic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We see now -- do you see line 3? I'll read it to you. Investigator Nicholls says in line 3: "We will tell you what this number is. We know that these documents are authentic because we received them directly from Republika Srpska. When we received them, we put a registration number --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is "directly from Republika Srpska." In the English version, we have "from VRS." There is, again, perhaps an interpretation problem or translation problem. I just wanted to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, this interview was done in English with Mr. Nicholls, and so he would have -- the English version is what would have come out of Mr. Nicholls' mouth. And it may have been the translator on site may have made the mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I just wanted to indicate that there is a problem of translation. Please carry on. Sorry for interrupting you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It continues: "When we get them, we stamp what's called an evidence registration number. That is our number just to keep track of evidence." Now, I want to ask you: These words about the authenticity of a document, could they have influenced you so that you accept -- take it for granted that a document is authentic?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I think it's authentic just because of my signature, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: But you never suspected that it's technically possible to scan your signature and then put it on a blank piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not have such suspicions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry for speaking first. At this point, I would like to object. And if Mr. Tolimir continues on this, I think he's obligated, under Rule 90(H), that in cross-examining a witness, he needs to put his case, his position, to the witness. So if he is, in fact -- it is his position that this is a falsified document, he needs to say that, under this Rule, as opposed to just going all around the issue. This Rule requires that you actually say that to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I don't mind this document at all. I could even have it admitted. The Prosecutor shouldn't worry about that. I just want to reach -- to get to the truth about the authenticity of particular documents. Let us go to page 6 of the Serbian version, lines 2 to 5, and English version page 7, where Mr. Nicholls says to the witness -- it says: "There are no surprises here, no tricks, nothing, no forgery. Forget what's written in the order, and I mean forget it. I want you to explain to me how it worked, these headings. This order would be sent," et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is that what Nicholls said to you in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did the Prosecution ask you anything about the contents of the documents during breaks in your interview in Sarajevo? Did you have any breaks?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: During these breaks, did you discuss documents at all; authenticity, anything?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now show P469. This is the cover page of the Atlantis telegram. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you see this on the left-hand side of the screen?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And on the right-hand side, you can also see "Atlantida," the translation into the Latinic script, and on the right-hand side [as interpreted] it's written in the Cyrillic script?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you explain whether what is written in the Cyrillic, this heading, "Atlantida," was written in the Rogatica Brigade by you and Ziza, or was this written by somebody else after the telegrams were placed in this cover and in the file, and when it was given this number that makes it authentic? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I am definitely not the one who wrote these words.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you see on this page where it says: "Telegrams 28/34"?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is this written in the Latin or the Cyrillic script?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: The Latin script.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: What about the heading; is that in the Cyrillic or the Latin script?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: "Atlantida" is written in the Cyrillic script.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now show document P469, page 2. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before this document disappears from the screen, could the witness please tell, if you recall, who has written the word "telegrami" on this cover page? Do you recognise this handwriting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I don't recognise that. The first time I saw this cover sheet was when it was shown to me in Sarajevo. That was the first time. I didn't see it before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then the other document should come up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you see this document, and what is it? What is it that you see? Can you explain, please?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I can see "Military Secret, Strictly Confidential," and then I can see the number "042," which is upside down, and I cannot read what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you see anything written in the Cyrillic, underneath "Military Secret"? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: The word "Vod," "Platoon," is written, definitely "Vod." I can't read this other word, the second word.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The document which has no content, is that something which would be marked with the words "Military Secret" and "Strictly Confidential"?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In your practice, would you put anything like "Military Secret, Strictly Confidential" on a document that didn't have any contents?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can remember, no, we wouldn't do that. That's -- that was not what we would do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you place the date, time, and place on a blank piece of paper when you sent the telegram or did you put that information on the contents of the telegram?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: We would do that on the contents of the telegram.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we look at page 2 of this document. Oh, we are looking at page 2. Can we now show document 122.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you see the document on the left? Is this something that was typed on your teleprinter, and did you process this document on your teleprinter and receive it? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And how did you mark it in the upper corner?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: The right-hand corner: "Received at 245 hours the 30th of July, 1995."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you always mark the documents in the upper right-hand corner, the time that you received it, the time you sent it, and put your signature there? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I would always say whether it was received, sent out, the time, the date, and the signature. The top part of the paper would always need to be marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm asking you, in the telegrams that were shown to you that are being tendered here through you, did you always sign in the upper right-hand corner of the paper?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. The couple that we looked at was signed in the right-hand corner, upper corner. Sometimes I signed it at the bottom of the page too.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at P472 now, please. Can we also look at P468 together with this document. Thank you. Page 9 in the English -- in the Serbian, page 9 in the Serbian, and page 12 in the English. Can we look at page 9 in the Serbian and page 12 in the English of document P468. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We see the part when you start speaking. This is the fourth line from the top. You say: "No. As a rule, this is not a telegram at all. You could not send this like this. There is no indication of to whom this is being sent to, for example." And then the other person says: "But this could be a document that was supposed to be sent to the field or is an order; what is it?" And then you say: "I don't know." Did I quote correctly what you said and what the Prosecutor said? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please, since during the war you did send telegrams, can you please point out to us what is missing on this telegram that we are looking at now? What is missing there? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: The person who is sending it is missing, and to whom it is being sent is also missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: A teleprinter operator, would he know to whom he should send this telegram and who it was received from? Would he know that?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No, he wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Would you add this telegram to your collection of telegrams, such as the collection "Atlantida" is, if you wish to keep a collection of telegrams for some purpose or other?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I would not include it in my collection.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we have the English up so we can see it for the testimony? It's hard to say what it -- I mean, Ms. Stewart's got it for me on her private one, but I think it's helpful to see that so we can understand what the questions have to do with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And we do see the English version, which is what the Prosecutor asked for. Can I continue, Your Honour? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to have an indication where, in the English translation of the interview of the witness, we found -- we will find this passage.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I asked the witness what was missing in this telegram so that the teleprinter would be able to process it and send it. He said that there was no heading and there was no addressee indicated. In English, that is in the transcript on page 12, where he talks with the -- thank you. And then he answered my question that he wouldn't know to whom he would send the telegram to - thank you - because there is no address that the teleprinter operator would be able to use. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Page 12, line 5 and the following. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, can you please tell us if you have to have an address to which you would send the telegram, and the address would need to have a technical means of receiving what you are sending to them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now look at Exhibit P481, page 2, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see the exhibit that I asked for on the left. The document is in the form of a telegram. However, do you see if something has been added by hand at the bottom of this page?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, item 7 has been added in handwriting. It's not typed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And would this look more like a draft telegram or a telegram, and was it permitted to add things like that by hand?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if I remember correctly, it wasn't, but I'm not really sure.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We see that this item 7 was not translated into English, but it's not important, in terms of this witness or for these proceedings in general. Can we look at 65 ter 124 on the screen now, please. Thank you. Thank you. Prosecutor's 65 ter 124 is not part of the "Atlantida" set of documents, as the representatives of the Prosecution marked it. This is Prosecutor's 65 ter number 124. Can we look at that one, please? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, there are some problems to find such a document. Do you perhaps mean the P number 124 instead of the 65 ter number? It can't be found.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was the Prosecutor's 65 ter number 124. Perhaps the Prosecutor can tell you where we can find it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, can you assist us?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, I can say that the document that is on the screen, which is P124, is part of the compact section of "Atlantida." We have the originals here, and the ERN numbers were done in the order that they were in the file. And that ERN number on this document is within the ERN range of the "Atlantida," so this particular document, which is on our list, is part of the "Atlantida" collection. Beyond that, I'm not sure where we went.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, can you help us?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. All I can say is the document, Prosecutor 65 ter 124, has number ERN 0293-5555. Thank you. This is a document on the accommodation of prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think he meant 65 ter 124, and that fits, and that is not a member of "Atlantida." So he just mixed up the now almost archaic 65 ter numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: He was referring to the 65 ter list of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That appears to be what, and we're slowly pushing that list to the side and replacing it with other numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I note, Mr. Tolimir, that you didn't indicate that you were going to use this document. If you do that in advance always, it would help everybody in the courtroom, especially the Registry, to find the document properly. I think we have it now on the screen. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Ms. Stewart says it is on his list. It was in a range of material. They did ask us just a few hours ago for the originals of this, which we have, if they need those. And, yes, it does have the 65 ter number for identification. But it's not in evidence yet, so it has never been -- gotten another number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you to Mr. McCloskey. Thank you, Mr. President. We did indicate this document last night.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can we now ask the witness to tell us whether he was the one who processed this document on the teletype and whether he confirmed its receipt with his signature on the 13th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, at 2230 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you indicate that in the upper right-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the question. The microphone was switched off.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you please look at the third line of this document, and you can see where it says the number there is still unclear. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what this number is? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: "8," and I think there's one "0" there. I'm not sure. I would say that it's "80."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now look at page 2 of this telegram. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you see on page 2 now, in line 5 of the text, the number that was unclear on the previous page?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what number that is and whether there was some kind of teleprinter error, typing error, or for some other reason, where the number is not the same?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Here we can see "8" and then most probably two "0s," "800 ."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So what should be written in the first document?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: It should be "800."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes, "800." All right, very well. It says -- in hand, it's written: "If you are not able to adequately accommodate all prisoners of war from Srebrenica, we inform you that in Sjemec, in the facilities of the 1st" something "Brigade, there is arranged accommodation," with an unintelligible word, "Palace [phoen], for 800 prisoners of war"?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You probably wrote this yourself?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: On this telegram written in hand, did you put any initials?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: You can't see them here. Probably not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you indicate when it was transmitted, when it was sent, on which date?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was it customary that you write that only on the teleprinter copy?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: If somebody wanted us to make a teleprinter copy, yes. But if we just returned it like this, we didn't write anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Look at the next page. We're again on page 1, and you put your signature and time sent on the teleprinter copy, not the copy that I gave you?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Would it have been normal to do the same with the Savcic telegram that was only typed on a typewriter, without a teleprinter copy?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, probably when somebody brought this telegram of yours, was it your telegram?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: That's not what I'm asking you. I'm asking you about the Savcic telegram. If you had a teleprinter copy, would you have signed the teleprinter copy or the one on the typewriter?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he maybe didn't want a copy. Maybe he just wanted to get back the copy that he gave me, and that's what I signed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The question was not heard. The microphone was off. The answer:

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, I suppose you did whatever your superior taught you to do. I didn't ask you for anything, because I'd never seen you and I never talked to you on the phone. But please don't worry about that. I'm only discussing what is logical. It would have been logical to have a teleprinter copy of what was written on a typewriter. Would it have been logical to have a teleprinter copy of the Savcic telegram typed on a typewriter, like you have the teleprinter copy of the telegram that I wrote in hand?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: There should be a teleprinter copy of the Savcic telegram.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, this document, the first and the second page, I would like to have admitted into evidence because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There's no need for giving a specific reason. It will be received. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: While we're still on this document, we just received the original, so it may be a good time for the General to look at it so he doesn't have to go back, if that's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, we agree.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 124 is now Exhibit D49.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. The Chamber would like to see it as well. It may be shown to the witness so that he can state for the record what he said to the versions on the screen. Do you recognise these two documents, one handwritten and one obviously from the teleprinter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do recognise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just to clarify, the handwritten version, is that written by you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean this one? No, I didn't write this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do you know who produced this? Whose handwriting is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whose handwriting it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You just received it and typed it into the teleprinter and sent it out; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. That might be given back to Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, now, a moment ago you had in your hand both the handwritten telegram and the teleprinter version. Were both signed by Major-General Zdravko Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't pay attention. I can have a look again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes, please. Can the telegrams be given to the witness again, because you said you didn't know who wrote them, for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it says "Z. Tolimir, Major-General, Assistant Commander." I'm not 100 per cent sure, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you please concentrate on item 1 of this telegram that you see on the left-hand side of the screen. Rather, the three lines above item 1. To answer this question, I'll read it to you: "If you are unable to find adequate accommodation for all prisoners of war from Srebrenica, we hereby inform you that in Sjemec, in the facilities of the 1st Light Infantry Brigade, there is arranged accommodation with tents for 800 prisoners of war."

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you write this on the teleprinter?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is this a notification, because in the second line it says "we hereby inform you"?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's a notification.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You are a native of Rogatica. Were there any sheep, or horses, or pigs in Sjemec, was there a farm?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were barns and stables, and there was -- there were sheep, cattle, pigs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: When did you send this?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: It was transmitted at 2230 on the 13th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this telegram. In fact, it's already exhibited. And now we move on to the next round of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's incumbent upon the General to provide some authentication for that. And under Rule 90(H), since he is cross-examining on it, his position on whether this is authentic and from him would be helpful to know, unless he chooses not to, but I think that would be helpful to know. And there is precedent that would suggest he must tell us, Rule 90(H), and when offering a document into evidence, its authentication should be attested to by the person offering it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we would like to receive your comment on that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I took a Prosecution document that the Prosecution marked 65 ter 124, and that he'd disclosed to the Defence. I tendered it like I tender any document. I do not make claims of authenticity when I tender documents. I'm not the accused here and I'm not being questioned here as a witness. I am tendering documents into evidence, and the Prosecution and the others can discuss it and take their positions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Based on what the General has said, I would object to this being -- coming into evidence, because I think it's an inappropriate precedent that a document comes into evidence with no attestation about authenticity, and of course, just because the Prosecution gave something to him doesn't mean anything. And I think he should say something about it, and if he's going to cross-examine him on it, he should say, under Rule 90(H). Now, yes, he is an accused representing himself, and that complicates the issue, I think. But when it comes to offering a document into evidence, I think he's required to say something more than, I don't have to say anything. To the degree of what he says, of course, is your -- in your view, but he must say something, in view of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the fact that the Prosecution has disclosed many documents to you and your Defence doesn't mean anything about the authenticity of these documents. It is an obligation of the Prosecution to give you all the documents related to this case. You are using now this document, and not the Prosecution. They didn't tender it, they didn't put it to the Chamber's knowledge. You did it. And, therefore, you should consider your position, although it's complicated for you, as you have no counsel but you are representing yourself. But for the fairness for the witness, especially, and for the fairness of the procedure, you should take into account the position of Mr. McCloskey so that we have a full picture what is happening during the examination of this witness. Would you like to have the second break now? Then you can consider the situation and confer with your legal assistant, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. But I confirmed, through this witness, that he sent this telegram. And he said in the right top corner he signed, that it was transmitted at 2230 hours on the 13 July 1995, so I'm introducing it through this witness. He confirmed he wrote it. I can write hundreds of documents in my own hand, whether they will be accepted by the Prosecution or not. I'm introducing it through the witness, and it's up to the witness to say whether it's authentic or not. I asked him whether the handwritten document is consistent with the contents of the telegram that he transmitted. Of course, he can be asked the same question by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That is sufficient, in the view of the Prosecution, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: As the document is already admitted as D49, I think we can leave this problem at this stage. Thank you very much. You have five minutes left before the second break, Mr. Tolimir. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Mr. President, and I thank the Prosecutor. Can we please call up 123, Exhibit 123. It's a document dated 13 July. It has a typewritten signature, "Zdravko Tolimir," and the title is: "The situation in the Zepa enclave."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is, in fact, P123.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, if you just look at this document, you will see that it was processed by your predecessor on your shift, and it's signed "Ziza" in the Serbian version, and even this teleprinter copy you sent to the Drina Corps. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In the top right corner, does it say "Copy" and "Ziza"?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In the bottom right corner, does it say "Transmitted at" and the time indication?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It is a matter of indifference to me whether it's "0050" or "950," so I'm not going to ask you anything about that. Can we conclude from this document that it was sent on the 13th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No, you can't conclude that. The date indicated in the heading is 13 July 1995, but it's not supported by any text below. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It doesn't matter. Does the heading say "13 July"?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does, "13 July 1995."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: At the beginning, we read: "This afternoon, we did not manage to establish the planned contacts with the representatives from Zepa, Torlak and Omanovic, as it had been scheduled to meet at 2100 hours. "They informed us through UNPROFOR that they were active during the day, informing the population about the conditions of their evacuation from Zepa, and they were forced to do that because the government in Sarajevo decided that they should not evacuate." Now, based on what I've just read, can we conclude from the document that it relates to the events of 12 July 1995, from this passage where it says: "This afternoon, we did not manage to establish contact as planned ..."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show document P491 to help the witness answer this question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's again a document sent on the 13th of July, 1995. The same title, "The situation in the Zepa enclave," under the name of Zdravko Tolimir. And we see in the right top corner that it was transmitted at 1820 hours on the 13th of July, and we see your signature in the right top corner.

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In the bottom corner, are these your initials?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: On the 13th, were you working, because you seem to have sent all the telegrams on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you now read the first sentence: "On 13 July 1995, at 1200 hours, we contacted Hamdija Torlak and Mujo Omanovic ..." Is that written in the first two lines?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We read a moment ago that we were not able to have contact on the 12th, and now in the 13th, in the telegram you sent, it says that the contact did take place on the 13th because they had talked to the population. Can we then conclude that the previous document relates to the 12th and this one to the 13th?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: This one relates to the 13th. Now, the previous one, where it says there was no contact, it could be the 12th. Maybe we can return that document back on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before we do that, one answer of the witness was not recorded because there was no verbal response. The witness was asked: "In the bottom corner, are these your initials?" And I think your answer was: "Yes, 'GD.'" Are these your initials?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you, just for the sake of the record. Let's have a look on the other document again to answer the question of Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P123. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's on the screen now, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You asked to see the document in order to be able to answer whether these two telegrams are linked by their contents and whether the contents from the telegram that we looked at earlier and the first sentence of this telegram refer to the same topic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they do refer to the same topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you said that I had five more minutes. I have finished with this section. If we need to go on a break, we can do that now, and then we can continue with part 2. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That's fine. We must have our second break now, and we will resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Our apologies for the delay. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, sir, we are going to move to a second set of questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And before that, could we please see document P125. Thank you. That's the document that was typed on a typewriter, which is allegedly the telegram sent by Savcic. Thank you, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We've seen in all the telegrams that we have been shown so far that you wrote in the upper right-hand corner when you received and sent the telegrams that we saw on the screen and that we looked at so far; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Only in this telegram, we see that what is written in the left lower-hand corner is: "Handed in at 1510 hours on the 13th of July, 1995," and your signature, and that that is a photocopy of your signature and the words that you wrote in; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you please tell me if you listened to the testimony of General Savcic here before this Tribunal over the internet, or did you follow it in the media because it was open and public? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Are you aware that in the Popovic case, General Savcic stated that he never wrote this telegram and that he never -- and that it never arrived in the battalion?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. General Savcic is on the witness list. But if he's going to make reference to the Popovic testimony, especially on something like this, he needs to provide line and page, because my memory is distinctly different from what he has said on that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, could you give a reference?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you to Mr. McCloskey. This is page 15262 of the transcript from the Popovic case. Since the witness doesn't understand English, I'm going to read the translation of a part of the transcript. It is 1D118, page 32, in the e-court. Thank you. Can we look at the English on one side and the Serbian on the other side so that the witness could, because he doesn't understand. Thank you. Can you put Savcic's document on one side and on the other side -- so on one side, you can put the Prosecutor's 65 ter 185, which is Exhibit P125, and on the other side can you put the transcript that Savcic is speaking. Thank you. Now I'm going to read lines 2 and 5 on page 15262. The Prosecutor asked Savcic: "Do you remember if you prepared this document?" And the witness, Savcic, replies on lines 7 to 14, I quote: "My name is there, but there is no signature, so I've already told you that that I don't recall drafting this document myself. And here are a few reasons why I still can't believe that I did. First of all, in the heading, it says 'IKM, forward command post of the 65th Protection Regiment,' et cetera, 'Borike, 1400 hours.' I did not set up that forward command post. I just led a part of the unit that was there. There is no date indicated. This document does not have the format of a telegram ..." And then on lines 16 and 17, he states, I quote Savcic: "Next, I cannot suggest something to the commander of the Main Staff or his deputy, because I'm not an assistant commander to suggest and propose anything. I'm just a subordinate who executes the orders given to him." Then Savcic says in lines 19 to 24, after the first sentence he says as follows: "'Assistant commander of the Main Staff of the VRS for intelligence and security proposes the following measures.'" This is what it says in the telegram after the first sentence: "So the assistant commander proposes, and I'm the one who writes. If he is the one proposing, then why he isn't -- isn't he the one who's writing?" Then I've just noticed the names of units start in small letters, not in capital letters. This is page 15263 of the transcript, and it is page 33 in e-court, lines 1, 5. And it goes on to, and I quote: "That's something that I know, so I cannot say with any certainty that I drafted this as dictated by Tolimir, but I cannot refute the possibility with 100 per cent certainty either. I can just say that this document was never received by the commander of the military police ..."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note: We no longer see the original on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "And the commander of the military police never acted upon it." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that the document on the left-hand side of the screen, if it was signed by Colonel Milomir Savcic, which he denies, would it also need to bear his signature?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Had it been typed, the name, wouldn't he need to sign the document?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I really cannot answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right, thank you. We understand each other. Can you please read what the first sentence of the telegram says, the telegram allegedly sent by Savcic? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: "In the sector of Dusanovo (Kasaba) ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. "In the sector of Dusanovo (Kasaba) over 1.000 [Realtime transcript read in error "100"] members of the former 28th Division of the so-called B and H Army were arrested. The prisoners are under the control of the Battalion of the Military Police of the 65th Protective Regiment."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: First we would like to have the English translation on the screen, on the right side, please. And, secondly, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's all I was trying to do. It's an important document. It's very difficult for the interpreters as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Absolutely. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir. I don't know, it appears that there are differences between the English translation we see on the screen and the translation we received on the record. For instance, "over 100 members," and if I look at the translation, there are "over 1.000 members." This is quite a difference. And in the original, it seems to be "1.000." I just wanted to point out that difference. There may be others. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. That's, of course, exactly the problem with not allowing the interpreters to see that. But this is an official CLSS translation of this document on the screen, so that should be the dispositive translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm sorry that I don't speak English, but I think that the interpreters, instead of saying the name "Dusanovo" first, they put it at the end. But I'm sorry, it's just a question of my not knowing English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is on the screen, and you should just carry on and put the next question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does the first sentence state or have the commander of the battalion allegedly inform the addressees about a certain situation in Dusanovo?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And does it say where this information was obtained and how does he know this information?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "As for the rest of the telegram, the assistant commander for security and intelligence affairs of the VRS Main Staff proposes the following measures:" Is that what the second sentence of the telegram says?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Can we now look at document P123. Thank you. Can we look at the document on the left-hand side of the screen, thank you, and then we will come back to this document again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You can see the document P123, and you can see here that it's from your brigade, and it's got such and such a number. It's sent to the Main Staff, the Sector for Intelligence, and the Command of the Drina Corps. It's also sent to the Command of the 65th Protection Motorised Regiment and the Command of the 68th Protection Regiment. And then the bottom is signed by Assistant Commander General-Major Zdravko Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could Tolimir write directly to the battalion commander, because as you see, it has his address and it says that he sent this order to him? Could he also deliver the measures that he allegedly proposed in the same way to him?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. How can I know that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But did Tolimir have the authority to directly address the commander of the battalion, as we can see from this telegram that he's addressing him in the heading, because it does say here: "To the Commander of the 65th Protection Motorised Regiment"? It's the second addressee from the bottom. Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: "The Command of the 65th Regiment."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: If he sent this telegram to him, could he also send a telegram to him in which he's suggesting measures? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether he could have done that or not. I really don't know what the structure was and who could issue orders to whom.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. If I'm writing a telegram here, sending it to the Command of the Protection Regiment, could I send them other contents, other than these ones, and also send them to the same address? Could I do that or not? Was I able to do that or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think these questions regarding who has the power or authority to do this or that, he's clearly answered he has no idea. And to be raising his voice at this point, shouting that question over and over again, is inappropriate. I know he doesn't mean it badly, but it's been asked and answered. This witness doesn't know about these things, and I would ask that the objection be sustained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I was concerned about the use of court time with this witness. You should perhaps focus on those matters the witness can really testify about. He clearly stated that this was beyond his area of responsibility. And we have not much time left, perhaps 10 or 15 minutes for your cross-examination, and we should try to finish with this witness today, because the Prosecution and you indicated a certain time for examination and I think we have reached the end of it. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, can you please tell me when this telegram that you see on the left side of the screen was written?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 13th of July, 1995, was when it was typed. I don't know when it was written.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: When was it handed in?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was at 0050 or 0950 hours. We don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: 0050, as you asserted first, was it written before the telegram in which I am asking for the prisoners to be sent to Sjemec? If they don't have anywhere to accommodate them, I'm informing them that there is a room at Sjemec?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could I send a telegram to the Protection Regiment --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand what the accused said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the interpreters didn't catch your question. Please repeat. "Could I send a telegram to the Protection Regiment," and what was the end of your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was I able to send to the Protection Regiment a telegram with the same contents as Savcic's telegram, and would you have had to send it if I had sent it to you for encryption?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that was my question, and that was the answer of the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you, based on this telegram that allegedly Savcic wrote, know to whom he was to send it, to which address? Does this typewritten paper, written on a typewriter, bear a heading?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Simply, can we get it back up on the screen so the witness knows what document you're talking about and the record is clear?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P125, please, so the witness can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does the telegram indicate the address to which you are to send it?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: What does it say?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Commander of the Main Staff of Republika Srpska Army, assistant commander for morale, religious, and legal affairs of the same Main Staff, commander of the Military Police Battalion of the 65th ZMTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does it say who is sending the telegram?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Forward command post of the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you see that Savcic says in the telegram that he did not manage to set up a forward command post --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could they slow down, please, both speakers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please don't overlap. The interpreters can't catch it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the accused please repeat the last question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I have to confess I made a mistake. I thought you had indicated that you need two hours. You have indicated three hours. You are not under time pressure. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Can we then show document P490. Thank you, we see the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you please look at the heading? Does it say "Command of the 1st PLBR"?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does it say which date it is, 15 July?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does the signature say "Commanders Lieutenant-Colonel Rajko Kusic and Lieutenant-Colonel M. Savcic"?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does it mean that back on the 15th, Savcic did not have a forward command post; instead, he used the command post of your brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does this telegram make it obvious where Savcic was located?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did Savcic and Kusic sign this telegram?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At least their names are indicated there. I don't know whether they signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Are they the authors of the contents of the telegram that you sent?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know if they authorised it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you get this from someone who brought it from town or from your brigade command?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe the command, maybe from the town. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Would you write telegrams on a teleprinter if you got it from someone from town?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: You mean a simple citizen? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you see in the heading "Command of the 1st" such and such "Brigade, strictly confidential, 15 July"?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you see that the contents were signed for by Rajko Kusic and Savcic, their names are typewritten?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does that tell the person who processes the telegram and who receives it -- it's sent to the Main Staff and to the forward command post. Does it tell the receiver that these two men are together?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: It might. How do I know?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I understand what you're saying. Thank you. How much time did the messenger need to bring a telegram from Borike, from the forward command post, to you, this telegram from Savcic?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: It was 20, 25 minutes by car.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you transmit this telegram at 2315 hours?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 15 July 1995, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. That evening, was it brought to you from Borike or was it brought earlier?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember when it was brought. But as soon as it was brought, it was transmitted immediately afterwards. That means it's probably -- it was probably brought that evening, but I cannot be certain about the time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have again P492, and that's where we'll wrap up for today. Could we also see the lower right corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: What is the time indicated here?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It's "14 July"; right?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does it say: "To the Command of the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment"?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We've just seen a telegram sent to the command on the 13th, the Command of the Protection Regiment, by Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Have we read here a telegram that says, We sent it on the 13th, and where it says, We established contact with Torlak and the others?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was it also sent from your teleprinter?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It says: "At 12.00, we had a meeting with Torlak and Omanovic." You sent this telegram at 1510 hours?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could Tolimir have written that telegram you sent at 1510?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: He could have, but maybe he didn't. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: If he met with Torlak at 12.00 and attended that meeting, was it then possible for him to write that telegram and send it to you from Boksanica by courier, having typewritten it as well, so that you were able to send it already at 1510?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how long that meeting was. Boksanica is far away. And from Rogatica, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Look again at P125. Judging by the form and contents, who wrote this telegram?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: It says "Lieutenant Colonel Milomir Savcic." Whether he wrote it, I don't know. That's what I see on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was it transmitted at 1510?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: How much time did you need to do your work and transmit it?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly to the minute, but perhaps 30 minutes, perhaps slightly more or slightly less. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. This telegram does not bear any proof that it is Savcic who sent it?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: His name is there. It was sent under his name. Whether it was sent by Milomir Savcic, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is it true that anyone can type the name of Milomir Savcic or anyone else?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is there anything that authenticates it as written by this signatory?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: There's just his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: On record before this Court, he says that he never set up a command post and he never wrote this telegram?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: That's what he says. I can only see that it's written -- signed "Milomir Savcic." That's how I processed it and sent it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That is a misstatement. We saw what he said. He did not say he never sent it. He said he didn't recall sending it. He couldn't exclude the possibility. He never said what the General just said, and it's inappropriate to make such a false statement to a witness like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Referring to another transcript, you should be very precise, Mr. Tolimir. Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I quoted that. It's on the transcript, and I'm not going to ask the witness about it because we don't have time to call it again into e-court. I only asked him a question in relation to what is evident on the screen. I asked him about authorisation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We shouldn't debate this problem. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please, Witness, do you know about this date, the 13th of July? Did you speak to Lieutenant-Colonel Savcic or no?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Have you ever talked to him during combat activities?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This completes my cross-examination. This confirms that this telegram could not even have been dictated by the person who allegedly signed it. Thank you for answering my questions, Witness. Thank you for coming before this Court. I wish you a safe journey and a good life. God bless you. Thanks to the interpreters, who were keeping with us because we were really in a hurry today. Thank you, Your Honours, for your understanding and patience and all the assistance on behalf of my Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, just to avoid a misunderstanding, it is up to the Chamber to give weight to the witness testimony today. We are not in agreement with conclusions by either party after a witness has given evidence. Mr. McCloskey, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Have you an indication? How much time do you need? Do you need more than five minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I may need more than five minutes, but -- yeah, it's hard to say five minutes, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just start, and we'll see what --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Witness, General Tolimir suggested just recently that you normally -- or that all the documents we've seen, you sign in the right-hand top corner, and it's only -- he's suggesting, it appears, that only it's the left bottom signature from the 13 July Savcic document, P125, that is different from those. That was on page 55, lines 10 through 20, and more recently, just in the last 10 or 15 minutes, he mentioned something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have a document which we have given a 65 ter number recently, Mr. President, in response to this issue. The number we have given it, for the purposes of court, is 6347. I bring it specifically as redirect to counter the assertion made by General Tolimir. So it is in e-court at 6347, and I would like to give the original to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, have you seen this document recently?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yesterday, in my office?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us -- we can see it's dated 31 July. Is your handwriting on it at all?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: It's there, "Transmitted," and then the indication of time, "0900, 31 July 1995," and my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And so is this like the Savcic document; you've signed it "Transmitted" down in the lower left corner?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell, from looking at this original document, whether the document you hold in your hand is typed from a typewriter or from a teleprinter?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: This was a typewriter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who is the -- we see that Lelek is the Chief of Staff. Was he the Chief of Staff of the Rogatica Brigade at the time?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you know where his office was in relation to yours in the Communications Section?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: The commands were some 60, 70 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So Lelek was in the command building, 60 or 70 metres from where you were in the communications building?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, I'm sorry, I don't know this -- those buildings very well, but are they separate buildings or is it one big building and separate parts of?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Communications were in one small building and the command was in one larger building, but they were separate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did Captain Lelek have a secretary?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: There was a secretary. Whether she was his personal secretary, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did the command staff, Lelek and the secretaries, have access to a regular typewriter over at the command building?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: There was a typewriter there in their building. Whether they had access to it, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I'll also note we see a signature on this document. Do you recognise who that signature is?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean what I wrote or this other signature?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good question. The one under "Lelek."

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't recognise whose signature it is, whether Lelek's or someone else's. I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If someone else had signed for Lelek, should there be an indication before the signature?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you say that again?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If someone had signed for Milan Lelek, should there be an indication of that at the signature block somehow?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recall sometimes seeing the word "Za" on the signature block and then a signature? The word "Za" meaning "For" in English?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: You mean during the war? I don't remember. But generally speaking, later I would have seen things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the round thing on this document is?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: A stamp, if we mean the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So is that the official stamp of the Rogatica Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Most probably, because it's affixed here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And like the Savcic document of 13 July, did you send this document and -- type it into the teleprinter and send it off at the -- as noted with your signature and time?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know why the Savcic document, 125, did not have a signature or a stamp like this one does?

utterances.speaker: DANKO GOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have about five or ten more minutes, and I know we'll get in trouble.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We're getting really in trouble because of the other trial. I think we have to adjourn now, and perhaps there are some questions by the Chamber as well, so that it is necessary to continue with this witness tomorrow. I apologise for that, but we have to continue tomorrow, Witness, Mr. Gojkovic. We have to adjourn now and resume tomorrow morning at 9.00 in the same courtroom. And just to let you know, you shouldn't contact either party about the content of your testimony here in The Hague today. Thank you very much for your understanding. We adjourn and resume tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
